Before a customer sees your website, reads your email, or clicks a link you shared, a quiet system has already done its work. Your domain name, such as yourcompany.com, points people to the right place. Your email settings tell other mail systems that a message really came from you. Choosing a Domain Name People Can Remember and Type A good domain name is short, easy to say out loud, and easy to spell after hearing it once. Imagine telling it to someone over the phone. If you need to explain hyphens, unusual spellings, or numbers written as words, it will cost you visits and emails that never arrive. A few practical guidelines: Match your business name where you can. They might be on a train, standing in line, or comparing options on the couch. If your website was designed for a large desktop monitor and then squeezed down to fit a phone, they will feel it: tiny text, buttons that are hard to tap, and menus that fight back. Mobile-first design flips that process around. In this post, we explain what mobile-first and responsive design actually mean, why they matter for small and mid-size businesses, and how to check whether your own site measures up. Responsive Design and Mobile-First: What Is the Difference? These two terms are often used together, but they describe different ideas. Responsive design means a single website adapts its layout to the screen it is viewed on. Columns stack, images resize, and navigation changes shape, all from the same code and the same web address. Mobile-first is a way of working. Designers and developers plan the small-screen experience first, then add layout and features as more space becomes available. The order matters. When you start with a large screen, it is easy to fill space with extras that later have to be hidden or crammed onto a phone. When you start small, you are forced to decide what is truly important, and that clarity usually improves the desktop version too. Why Mobile-First Matters for Your Business A mobile-first approach is not just a technical preference. It affects how customers experience your brand and how search engines evaluate your site. Yet within moments of landing on a page, people form an impression of your business, and much of that impression comes from type and color. Crisp, readable text and a calm, consistent palette signal care and competence. Cramped lines, clashing colors, and five different fonts suggest the opposite, even when the services behind them are excellent. You do not need to become a designer to make better decisions here. Understanding a few principles will help you brief a design team, evaluate proposals, and keep your website consistent as it grows. Start With Readability, Not Personality It is tempting to choose fonts and colors based on mood first. A better order is to make sure everything is easy to read, then add personality within those limits. On a website, text is the product: it is how visitors learn what you do, what it costs, and how to contact you. A few readability fundamentals apply to almost every site: Body text size: Around 16 pixels is a common baseline for body copy on screens, and larger is often better for content-heavy sites or older audiences. Line height: Text set with line spacing of roughly 1.4 to 1.6 times the font size is far easier to read than tightly packed lines. Line length: Lines that stretch across a wide monitor are tiring to follow. Many designers aim for roughly 50 to 75 characters per line for English text. Alignment: Left-aligned text is usually easiest to scan in English. Fully justified text can create uneven gaps between words on the web. Or someone with a tremor who navigates with a keyboard instead of a mouse. Or an older visitor who simply needs larger, higher-contrast text. If your website works for them, it is accessible. Accessibility can sound like a technical specialty, but its foundations are surprisingly practical. This post explains the standard most of the world uses, why it matters for every business, and what you can check on your own site this week. What Is WCAG? The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, or WCAG, are published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), the organization that develops many core web standards. The current version is WCAG 2.2, released in October 2023. The guidelines are organized into three conformance levels: Level A: The minimum. Failing these makes content unusable for some people. Level AA: The level most organizations and many laws aim for. It covers the barriers that affect the largest number of users. Level AAA: The highest level, often not achievable for every type of content, and usually applied selectively. For most business websites, Level AA is the sensible target. In the United States, the Americans with Disabilities Act is widely applied to business websites, and WCAG is the usual measure. Many other countries have their own accessibility rules as well. pages.x: Security Nov 11, 2026 · 5 min read Website Security Essentials: A Practical Checklist for Small Businesses It is easy to assume that hackers only go after banks and large corporations. In reality, most attacks on websites are automated. Bots scan the internet around the clock looking for outdated software, weak passwords, and misconfigured servers. They do not care how big your company is; they care whether your site has an open door. A compromised website can show spam to your customers, redirect them to scam pages, leak form submissions, or be flagged by browsers as unsafe. The encouraging news is that a handful of consistent habits prevent the large majority of everyday problems. Think of website security not as one big lock, but as several layers, each one making the next attack harder. Layer One: Encrypt Everything With HTTPS HTTPS encrypts the connection between your visitor's browser and your website, so information like contact form entries and login details cannot be read or altered in transit. It relies on an SSL/TLS certificate installed on your server. What to check: Every page on your site loads with https:// , not just the checkout or contact page. Visitors who type http:// are automatically redirected to the secure version. Your certificate renews automatically. Free certificates from Let's Encrypt, offered by many hosts, typically renew every 90 days, and an expired certificate triggers alarming browser warnings. There is no "mixed content," meaning images or scripts still loading over plain HTTP. Modern browsers label non-HTTPS pages as "Not secure," so this layer protects your reputation as much as your data.
